title: Bonding
description: Connect orbital models to molecular geometry and reactivity.

review.note: Original explanations and exercises; source-backed author review, not independent expert verification.

cards.rule:
n = 1,2,… sets the shell. l = 0,…,n−1 sets the subshell (s,p,d,f). mₗ = −l,…,+l labels orbitals; mₛ = ±1/2 labels electron spin. Each orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.

In the usual multielectron-atom model, subshell energies within one shell increase s < p < d < f (for subshells allowed in that shell). In the nonrelativistic hydrogen-like model, orbitals with the same n have equal energy; do not apply the multielectron splitting to that model.
cards.cue: One s orbital; three p orbitals; five d orbitals; seven f orbitals. A p subshell can hold six electrons. For hydrogen-like atomic orbitals: total nodes = n−1; angular nodes = l; radial nodes = n−l−1. A 3p orbital has one angular node and one radial node.
cards.trap: Orbital phase signs are wavefunction signs, not positive and negative electric charges. Electrons do not orbit like planets. s orbitals have spherical angular symmetry; a p orbital has two lobes separated by a nodal plane. Higher-n orbitals may also have radial nodes. A node is a zero of the wavefunction, not a place where an electron waits.
cards.app: Carbon bonding uses valence orbitals from the second shell. Hybridization is a model for bonding and geometry, not a change in the allowed quantum numbers.

steps.label: 1. Count valence electrons
steps.text: The molecular drawing is ethene, H₂C=CH₂, shown as a later bonding example. The separate box diagram describes an isolated neutral carbon atom: 1s²2s²2p², with four valence electrons in the n=2 shell. Do not interpret the C=C lines as orbital boxes or apply the isolated-atom occupancy directly to a bonded carbon.

diagram.caption: Isolated neutral carbon, ground-state filling: 1s² 2s² 2p². This atomic model is distinct from the ethene bonding example.

steps.label: 2. Fill degenerate orbitals
steps.text: In the isolated-carbon box diagram, the two 2p electrons occupy separate degenerate orbitals with parallel spins (Hund’s rule). Electrons paired in a single orbital have opposite spins (Pauli exclusion). Ethene is the molecular example above; its bonding orbitals are a different model, developed in the next lesson.

diagram.caption: Isolated neutral carbon, ground-state filling: 1s² 2s² 2p². This atomic model is distinct from the ethene bonding example.

rule.title: Quantum Numbers (n, l, m_l, m_s), Nodal Planes & Ground-State Electron Configurations
rule.formula: Total Nodes = n − 1     |     Angular Nodes = l     |     Radial Nodes = n − l − 1

items.label: Aufbau, Pauli & Hund Rules
items.text: Fill lowest energy first (n+l rule); max 2 e⁻ per orbital with opposite spins; fill degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins.

items.label: Cation Formation & d-Block Exceptions
items.text: Remove electrons from HIGHEST n shell first (4s before 3d in Fe²⁺); remember Cr ([Ar] 4s¹3d⁵) and Cu ([Ar] 4s¹3d¹⁰).

figure.caption: Isolated carbon-atom spin occupancy model, not a molecular structure or an energy-scale diagram.

cue.title: Quantum Number & Ion Electron Configuration Checklist
cue.prompt: Which atomic orbital rule are you applying?

items.label: Counting Nodes in Any Orbital (e.g., 3p)
items.outcome: Total = n−1 (2); Angular = l (1); Radial = n−l−1 (1)
items.text: l = 0 (s), 1 (p), 2 (d), 3 (f). Angular nodes are flat planes/cones; radial nodes are spherical shells.

items.label: Forming a Transition-Metal Cation (e.g., Fe²⁺)
items.text: Neutral Fe is [Ar] 4s²3d⁶, so Fe²⁺ loses its two 4s electrons first → [Ar] 3d⁶ (4 unpaired electrons, paramagnetic).

items.label: Checking Pauli vs. Hund Violation
items.outcome: Same 4 Quantum Numbers = Pauli; Paired Too Early = Hund
items.text: Two arrows ↑↑ in the same box violates Pauli Exclusion; pairing ↑↓ in px while py is empty is an excited state (Hund).

trap.title: Removing 3d Electrons Before 4s in Transition Metal Ions

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Writing Fe²⁺ as [Ar] 4s²3d⁴ by subtracting from 3d instead of the outermost n=4 shell.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Once 3d orbitals are occupied, 4s is higher in energy and furthest from the nucleus: always ionize 4s electrons first!

app.title: Paramagnetic MRI Contrast Agents (Gd³⁺) & Hemoglobin Iron Spin States

items.label: Paramagnetic vs Diamagnetic
items.text: Any atom/ion with ≥1 unpaired electron (↑) is paramagnetic; all-paired (↑↓) is diamagnetic.

items.label: Hemoglobin Fe²⁺ Coordination
items.text: O₂ binding to heme Fe²⁺ shifts the iron spin state and pulls Fe²⁺ into the porphyrin plane.

items.label: Spectroscopy Selection Rules
items.text: For many first-row transition-metal cations, 4s electrons are removed before 3d. Orbital energies depend on occupancy and ionization; this is not a universal radial-distance rule.

cards.rule:
A sigma bond has electron density along the internuclear axis. A pi bond comes from side-on p-orbital overlap. A double bond has one sigma and one pi; a triple bond has one sigma and two pi. Constructive overlap forms a lower-energy bonding MO; destructive overlap gives an antibonding MO with an added node.

For comparable carbon–carbon bonds, an individual pi contribution is generally weaker than the sigma contribution because side-on overlap is less effective. Nevertheless, a double bond and a triple bond are generally stronger and shorter overall than a single bond. Their strength increments are unequal; do not add universal, context-free sigma and pi energies.
cards.cue: Bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons)/2 in the simple MO model. More bond order usually means shorter, stronger bonds for a given atom pair.
cards.trap: A pi bond restricts rotation because twisting disrupts overlap. Bond rotation is possible only by paying an energy cost; do not imagine a double bond freely rotating at room temperature.
cards.app: Carbonyl addition converts a pi bond into sigma bonds. Following sigma and pi electrons helps explain the change from planar to tetrahedral geometry.

steps.label: 1. Double bond inventory
steps.text: Ethene has one C–C sigma bond, one C–C pi bond, and four C–H sigma bonds: five sigma and one pi overall. The H₂C and CH₂ labels show the hydrogens; the four C–H bonds are not drawn as separate lines.

steps.label: 2. Triple bond inventory
steps.text: Ethyne has one C–C sigma plus two perpendicular pi bonds. Each CH label includes one hydrogen whose C–H bond is not drawn separately. Add those two C–H sigma bonds: three sigma and two pi overall.

rule.title: Sigma (σ) vs. Pi (π) Overlap, Bond Order & Molecular Orbital (MO) Theory
rule.formula: Bond Order = ½ (Bonding e⁻ − Antibonding e⁻*)     |     Double Bond = 1σ + 1π     |     Triple Bond = 1σ + 2π

items.label: Head-On (σ) vs. Side-by-Side (π)
items.text: Head-on σ overlap concentrates electron density directly between nuclei (stronger individual bond) and permits 360° rotation.

items.label: Antibonding Orbitals (σ*, π*)
items.text: Populating an antibonding orbital creates a nodal plane between the nuclei, lowering bond order and lengthening the bond.

comparison: Adds node between nuclei; weakens bond

figure.caption: Bonding-orbital overlap schematic. Lobe colors denote phase, not electric charge or electron paths.

cue.title: Fast Sigma & Pi Bond Counting Formula for Any Graph
cue.prompt: What bond property are you comparing?

items.label: Counting Total σ and π Bonds
items.outcome: Every Atom-Atom Link = 1σ; Extra Lines = π
items.text: Remember to count implicit C–H σ bonds! A double bond adds +1π; a triple bond adds +2π.

items.label: Individual σ vs. π Bond Strength
items.text: The π bond is weaker and higher in energy (HOMO), making alkenes nucleophilic in addition reactions.

items.label: Total Bond Energy & Bond Length
items.outcome: C≡C > C=C > C–C Strength; C≡C < C=C < C–C Length
items.text: Higher bond order (3 > 2 > 1) pulls nuclei closer together and requires more total energy to cleave completely.

trap.title: Forgetting Implicit C–H Bonds When Counting Total σ Bonds

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Counting only the visible C–C skeleton lines in skeletal structures and missing all the C–H σ bonds.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Expand every carbon to 4 total bonds first (or use Total σ = Total Atoms − 1 + Rings) so every C–H σ bond is included.

app.title: HOMO–LUMO Transitions in Conjugated Polyenes & Electrophilic Addition

items.label: Alkene Nucleophilicity
items.outcome: π-Bond Is the HOMO Electron Source
items.text: Because π electrons sit further from the nuclei than σ electrons, HBr or Br₂ attacks the exposed π cloud while the σ frame stays intact.

items.label: Sn2 Backside Attack Angle
items.text: Attack occurs at 180° opposite the leaving group because that is where the large lobe of the C–LG σ* antibonding orbital points!

items.label: Conjugation & UV-Vis Shift
items.text: Adding conjugated π bonds narrows the HOMO–LUMO energy gap, shifting absorption toward longer, visible wavelengths.

cards.rule: Typical tetrahedral carbon is sp³ (about 109.5°), trigonal planar carbon is sp² (about 120°), and linear carbon is sp (180°). The s character is 25%, 33%, and 50%, respectively. Resonance contributors differ only in electron placement, not atom connectivity.
cards.cue: For ordinary carbon: four electron domains → sp³; three → sp²; two → sp. A multiple bond counts as one domain.
cards.trap: Do not mechanically label an amide nitrogen sp³ just because it has three sigma bonds and a lone pair. Its lone pair occupies a p orbital conjugated with the carbonyl, making the amide approximately planar.
cards.app: Peptide-bond resonance restricts C–N rotation. Delocalized charge explains carboxylate stability and why its two C–O bonds are equivalent in the resonance hybrid.

steps.label: 1. Carbonyl geometry
steps.text: The carbonyl carbon has three sigma-bond directions and a p orbital for the pi bond: sp² and approximately planar. Its methyl neighbor is sp³.

challenge.explanation: B is the carbonyl carbon with three electron domains.

steps.label: 2. Amide conjugation
steps.text: Nitrogen donates lone-pair electron density into the carbonyl system. The C–N bond has partial double-bond character; amide nitrogen is much less basic than a typical amine.

steps.label: 3. Resonance hybrid
steps.text: This drawing is one contributor of acetate. The other exchanges the two oxygen bond orders and the negative charge. The actual ion has delocalized charge; it does not flip back and forth between drawings.

rule.title: Hybridization, % s-Character, Bond Lengths & Resonance Delocalization Rules

items.label: Count Steric Number (σ Bonds + Localized Lone Pairs)
items.text: 4 domains = sp³ (109.5° tetrahedral); 3 domains = sp² (120° trigonal planar); 2 domains = sp (180° linear).

items.label: Resonance Hybridization Override
items.text: A lone pair adjacent to a π bond (amides, esters, aniline, pyrrole) rehybridizes from sp³ → sp² to sit in an unhybridized p orbital!

items.label: Percent s-Character Trend
items.text: sp (50% s) > sp² (33% s) > sp³ (25% s): higher s-character holds electrons closer to the nucleus → shorter bonds & stronger acidity.

figure.caption: Conjugated amide and carboxylate examples. A flat drawing does not measure bond angles.

cue.title: Resonance & Lone-Pair Hybridization Detector
cue.prompt: Does the heteroatom lone pair participate in resonance?

items.label: Next to a π Bond (Amide, Aniline, Ester)
items.outcome: Rehybridizes to sp² (Lone Pair in p Orbital!)
items.text: Delocalizing the lone pair into the adjacent π system lowers energy, making amide C–N bonds planar and non-basic.

items.label: Atom ALREADY Has a π Bond (Pyridine N)
items.outcome: Lone Pair Stays in sp² Hybrid Orbital!
items.text: Because pyridine nitrogen already uses its p orbital for the aromatic ring π bond, its lone pair sits orthogonal in an sp² orbital (basic!).

items.label: No Adjacent π System (Alkyl Amine RNH₂)
items.text: Localized lone pair occupies an sp³ hybrid orbital and is freely available to accept a proton.

trap.title: Calling Amide Nitrogen sp³ or Moving Atoms Between Resonance Structures

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Counting 3 σ bonds + 1 lone pair on an amide nitrogen and calling it sp³ trigonal pyramidal.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Amide, ester, and aniline heteroatoms are sp² trigonal planar because their lone pair delocalizes into the adjacent π system!

app.title: Peptide Bond Planarity, Terminal Alkyne Acidity & Carboxylate Equivalence

items.label: Peptide Backbone Rigidity
items.outcome: Amide C–N Has Partial Double-Bond Character
items.text: Resonance locks all 6 atoms of the peptide link in a rigid plane, governing α-helix and β-sheet folding.

items.label: Terminal Alkyne Deprotonation
items.text: NaNH₂ cleanly deprotonates RC≡CH to form an acetylide nucleophile because 50% s-character stabilizes the carbanion.

items.label: Carboxylate Resonance Hybrid
items.text: Deprotonating RCOOH spreads −1 charge equally over two electronegative oxygens, lowering pKa to ~4.8.

stages.prompt: For a 2p electron, which n and l pair is allowed?
stages.explanation: p means l=1; with n=2, l may be 0 or 1.
hints: p is the subshell after s.

stages.prompt: How many orbitals are in a p subshell?
How many electrons can a filled p subshell hold?
stages.explanation: Three orbitals times two electrons each gives six.
hints: Each orbital holds two opposite-spin electrons.

stages.prompt: For a hydrogen-like 3p orbital, how many radial nodes are present?
stages.explanation: For 3p, n=3 and l=1. Radial nodes = n−l−1 = 1.
hints: Subtract l and one from n.

stages.prompt: How many angular nodes does that 3p orbital have?
stages.explanation: Angular nodes = l. A p orbital has l=1, giving one angular node (a plane).
hints: Use the subshell letter rather than n.

stages.prompt: In the usual multielectron-atom model, which listed n=3 subshell is lowest in energy?
stages.explanation: Within one shell in the usual multielectron model, s < p < d. In the nonrelativistic hydrogen-like model these same-n orbitals are degenerate.
hints: Use the within-shell order s < p < d.

exercises.summary: Atomic models: allowed quantum numbers, p-subshell capacity, hydrogen-like node counts, and multielectron subshell energy order. The molecular example is ethene.
exercises.context: The ethene drawing is a companion bonding example only. These questions concern atomic orbitals and subshells, not the total electrons or molecular orbitals of C2H4. No atomic filling diagram is supplied during this workshop.
